hints: Focus on where the OH group sits, because dehydration removes OH plus one H from a neighbouring carbon to make a C=C bond.
For each alcohol, list the different neighbouring carbons that have H atoms, each unique neighbour can give a different structural alkene.
Remember to check each alkene for E/Z isomerism, a C=C with two different groups on each end counts as two different alkenes.
walkthrough:
**Recall how dehydration works**

Think of dehydration as pulling off the OH and one nearby H to form water. The double bond forms between the C that had OH and the C that lost H.

$$\text{R-CH(OH)-CH}_2\text{-R'} \rightarrow \text{R-CH=CH-R'} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Count structural alkenes for each alcohol**

Look at the carbons next to the C-OH. In A, a primary $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$, there is only one neighbour with H, so only one alkene. In D, also primary $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, again only one alkene. In B, hexan-3-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, there are two different neighbours, giving hex-2-ene and hex-3-ene. In C, 3-methylpentan-3-ol, there are also two types, giving 3-methylpent-2-ene and 2-ethylbut-1-ene.

**Add E/Z stereoisomers**

A C=C counts twice if each C of the double bond has two different groups. Both hex-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and hex-3-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, show E and Z forms, so B gives $2 + 2 = 4$ alkenes. For C, 3-methylpent-2-ene shows E and Z, but the terminal alkene $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_2\text{CH}_3)_2$ does not, so C gives $2 + 1 = 3$ alkenes.

**Pick the greatest**

A gives 1, D gives 1, C gives 3, and B gives 4. So the hexan-3-ol isomer gives the greatest number of different alkenes.

options.A: This is 2,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol, $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The OH is on C1 and only C2 has H to lose, giving only $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3)\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_3$. It is terminal so no E/Z isomerism, only 1 alkene in total.
options.B: This is hexan-3-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Loss of H from either side gives two structural alkenes, hex-2-ene and hex-3-ene. Both are non-terminal with two different groups on each C=C carbon, so each exists as E and Z, giving 4 different alkenes in total, the most.
options.C: This is 3-methylpentan-3-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(CH}_3)\text{(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. It gives two structural alkenes: 3-methylpent-2-ene and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(=CH}_2)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Only the first shows E/Z isomerism, so total is 3, fewer than option B.
options.D: This is 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol, $\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The OH is primary with only one neighbouring $\text{CH}_2$ group, giving only $\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{CCH=CH}_2$. No E/Z is possible, so only 1 alkene.
